title: Phase 1: Time-Limited Elimination (2-6 Weeks)
subtitle: Strict, temporary removal of high-FODMAP foods to establish a clean symptom baseline.
purpose: Identify whether fermentable carbohydrates are driving your IBS symptoms.
key_steps: Replace high-FODMAP staples with certified low-FODMAP alternatives.
Maintain a detailed food and daily symptom log.
Assess symptom reduction at week 4.
common_mistakes: Staying on strict elimination for months or years (damages microbiome diversity).
Fearing trace ingredients while ignoring major triggers.
Assuming low-FODMAP means gluten-free or dairy-free.
dietitian_tip: If symptoms do not improve by week 6, re-evaluate with a Registered Dietitian; continuing restriction beyond 6 weeks without benefit is counterproductive.

title: Phase 2: Systematic Reintroduction & Challenge
subtitle: Testing individual FODMAP groups step-by-step to discover exact threshold limits.
purpose: Identify which specific FODMAP groups trigger symptoms and at what exact serving size.
key_steps: Test one FODMAP group at a time (e.g., Fructans, Sorbitol, Lactose).
Consume a challenge food in increasing portions over 3 days (e.g. Day 1: 1/4 clove garlic; Day 2: 1/2 clove; Day 3: 1 full clove).
Take a 2-3 day washout period between test groups until symptoms return to baseline.
common_mistakes: Testing during a high-stress week or travel.
Testing two FODMAP groups simultaneously.
Giving up on a food group permanently after a single mild reaction.
dietitian_tip: Keep a baseline low-FODMAP diet during washout days to ensure clear results for the next challenge group.

title: Phase 3: Long-Term Personalization
subtitle: Re-expanding your diet to maximize microbiome health and dining freedom.
purpose: Enjoy a broad, nutritious diet containing only minimal restrictions for proven personal triggers.
key_steps: Reincorporate all well-tolerated FODMAP groups into daily meals.
Eat foods you reacted to in reduced, tolerable portion sizes.
Periodically re-test foods you previously failed (gut tolerance changes over time).
common_mistakes: Never attempting to re-test failed foods.
Labeling entire food groups as 'poison'.
dietitian_tip: Gut microbiome diversity thrives on 30+ different plant foods per week. Personalization is about freedom, not restriction!

title: Low-FODMAP Eating Out & Social Dining
subtitle: Practical strategies for restaurants, dinner parties, and social occasions.
purpose: Maintain digestive peace without sacrificing social life or feeling isolated.
key_steps: Review restaurant menus online beforehand.
Opt for simple grilled protein (steak, chicken, fish) with steamed vegetables or roasted potatoes.
Ask sauces and dressings to be served on the side.
Politely inform staff about garlic and onion sensitivity.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'gluten-free' menu items are garlic/onion free.
Skipping meals before dining out (causes hypoglycemia and exaggerated gastrocolic reflex).
dietitian_tip: Carry garlic/onion-free salad dressing packets or enzyme supplements when dining at unknown venues.

title: Travel, Flying & Road Trips with IBS
subtitle: Navigating airports, flight delays, and foreign cuisine with digestive confidence.
purpose: Prevent travel-induced flare-ups driven by flight pressure, dehydration, and schedule changes.
key_steps: Pack safe low-FODMAP portable snacks (macadamia nuts, rice cakes, dark chocolate, firm bananas).
Stay hydrated with plain water; avoid carbonated beverages on flights.
Pack an emergency gut toolkit (peppermint oil, loperamide, osmotic laxative, heating patch).
common_mistakes: Relying on airport fast-food kiosks.
Holding bowel movements on long flights.
dietitian_tip: Air cabin pressure changes cause intestinal gas expansion; stick to light, low-FODMAP meals 4 hours before boarding.

title: Reading Food Labels & Hidden FODMAPs
subtitle: How to spot sneaky fructans, polyols, and high-FODMAP additives in packaged foods.
purpose: Confidently scan ingredient lists in supermarket aisles in under 10 seconds.
key_steps: Check ingredient order: ingredients are listed by weight from highest to lowest.
Watch out for 'natural flavorings', 'dehydrated garlic/onion', 'inulin', 'chicory root', and 'high-fructose corn syrup'.
Be aware of sugar alcohols ending in '-ol' (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol, maltitol).
common_mistakes: Assuming 'organic' or 'vegan' products are low FODMAP.
Ignoring inulin / chicory root fiber added to high-protein snacks.
dietitian_tip: If garlic or onion powder is listed near the very end of ingredients (<2%), it may be tolerable for some, but avoid during strict elimination.

title: Balancing Fiber & Prebiotics in IBS
subtitle: Navigating soluble vs insoluble fiber for IBS-C and IBS-D.
purpose: Optimize stool consistency without triggering excessive bacterial gas.
key_steps: Understand the difference: Soluble fiber absorbs water into gel (great for both IBS-C & IBS-D); Insoluble fiber adds roughage.
Introduce soluble fiber (e.g. Psyllium husk, chia seeds, oats) slowly, titrating over 2 weeks.
Drink an extra glass of water with every fiber increase.
common_mistakes: Adding coarse wheat bran to constipation (insoluble roughage can worsen IBS pain).
Increasing fiber rapidly in one day.
dietitian_tip: Psyllium husk (isabgol) titrated to 5-10g daily is clinically proven to improve global IBS symptoms.

title: The Mind-Gut Axis & Stress Management
subtitle: How central nervous system stress directly triggers gut motility and pain sensitivity.
purpose: Calm the vagus nerve and reduce visceral hypersensitivity using mind-body interventions.
key_steps: Practice 10 minutes of daily gut-directed meditation or diaphragmatic breathing.
Utilize gut-directed hypnotherapy programs (e.g., Nerva protocol).
Maintain consistent sleep hygiene.
common_mistakes: Treating IBS solely as a dietary disease while ignoring severe stress triggers.
Hyper-fixating on food fear and anxious logging.
dietitian_tip: Research shows gut-directed hypnotherapy matches the efficacy of the low-FODMAP diet for long-term IBS symptom reduction!

title: IBS and Hormones / Menstrual Cycle
subtitle: Understanding why gut symptoms fluctuate across the luteal and menstrual phases.
purpose: Anticipate cycle-related flares and adjust self-care proactively.
key_steps: Track symptoms alongside menstrual cycle phases.
Prepare for progesterone drops before period start (often triggers loose stools and cramping).
Use heat therapy and gentle soluble fiber during pre-menstrual days.
common_mistakes: Blaming new food triggers when flares are actually driven by prostaglandins.
Over-restricting diet during pre-menstrual craving phases.
dietitian_tip: Increased bowel urgency right before or during your period is driven by uterine prostaglandins relaxing smooth muscles in both uterus and bowel.

title: Working with a Registered Specialist Dietitian
subtitle: Why professional guidance dramatically improves low-FODMAP success rates.
purpose: Ensure nutritional adequacy, prevent unnecessary restriction, and streamline reintroduction.
key_steps: Confirm practitioner credentials (Registered Dietitian / Registered Dietitian Nutritionist specializing in GI health).
Bring 3-7 days of food and symptom logs to initial consultation.
Collaborate on a tailored reintroduction calendar.
common_mistakes: Consulting unaccredited 'nutrition coaches' who order unvalidated IgG food sensitivity blood tests.
Attempting complex protocol management without expert baseline screening.
dietitian_tip: Always rule out coeliac disease (via IgA tTG blood test while eating gluten) BEFORE starting a low-FODMAP or gluten-free diet!
